stances.claim: The Constitution requires SBN justices to determine probable cause personally -- they cannot rely on the prosecutors say-so -- and this double determination check exists to curb abuses of prosecutors who indiscriminately file criminal charges.
stances.rhetorical_move: Charter-mandated-double-check framing of judicial probable cause

stances.claim: Once the SBN finds probable cause in plunder, the accused will be arrested and detained indefinitely (because plunder is punishable with reclusion perpetua and bail is denied when evidence of guilt is strong) -- detention pending trial is not a penalty but a flight-prevention measure.
Celebrities and other VIPs will fight for confinement in the more comfortable NBI/PNP detention facilities or seek house/hospital arrest -- the place of detention will be another battlefield.
Napoles or Dennis Cunanan, having failed to secure state-witness status from the OOO, may still seek it from the SBN during trial under Rule 119 Sec 17, provided they satisfy the five requirements.

notable_anecdotes: The three-division raffle outcome catalogued with full chair-and-member listings (Dela Cruz/Ponferrada/Lagos got Revilla; Tang/Quiroz/Martires got Enrile; Jurado/Gesmundo/Quiroz got Jinggoy) -- the most procedurally detailed assignment-roster in the corpus for the PDAF prosecution.
The Fifth Division vacancy quirk -- Quiroz concurrently serving Third and Fifth -- flagged as a temporary anomaly awaiting a new appointee, the kind of micro-procedural detail CJP routinely captures.

Verbatim quotation of Rule 119 Sec 17 five state-witness requirements -- applied forward-looking to Napoles and Cunanan as candidates, a rare instance of CJP forecasting which accused will likely attempt which procedural move.
The detention-place forecast -- house/hospital arrest as the VIP fight -- written in May 2014 before the actual Enrile/Revilla/Jinggoy detention-place skirmishes materialized.

one_paragraph_summary: Two days after the Office of the Ombudsman filed plunder and graft (Sec 3-e Anti-Graft Law) informations against Senators Bong Revilla, Juan Ponce Enrile, and Jinggoy Estrada, Janet Lim Napoles, and several others, Panganiban turns the spotlight on the Sandiganbayan. He walks the reader through the interlocutory orders that must precede trial proper: the three-division raffle (already done -- First Division of Dela Cruz/Ponferrada/Lagos got Revilla, Third of Tang/Quiroz/Martires got Enrile, Fifth of Jurado/Gesmundo/Quiroz got Jinggoy, with Quiroz concurrent Third/Fifth); the Charter-mandated double determination of probable cause (the judges cannot rely on the prosecutors say-so but must personally peruse the information, affidavits, and evidence, a check designed to curb prosecutorial abuses); the right to bail (granted as a matter of right except in capital offenses like plunder when the evidence of guilt is strong, with detention pending trial framed as a flight-prevention measure rather than a penalty); and the place of detention (the VIP fight for NBI/PNP comfortable facilities or house/hospital arrest, against the normal city/provincial jail). He forecasts the further skirmishes -- motions to quash for defective information, postponement motions, medical-treatment requests, opposition to suspension-from-office under the Plunder Law -- and singles out Napoles and Dennis Cunanan as likely candidates to seek state-witness discharge from the SBN under Rule 119 Sec 17, having failed at the OOO. The five Rule 119 requirements (absolute necessity, no other direct evidence, substantial corroboration, not most guilty, no moral-turpitude conviction) are quoted in full. He closes with the CIPI standard: the spotlight will be focused on the SBN's competence, integrity, probity, and independence.
